headline: High risk: Gemini CLI can write/egress by default while awesome-nlp is non-runnable, so interaction risks center on filesystem/MCP misuse and compliance gaps.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-nlp is a non-runnable open-source list with no I/O surfaces, so it cannot itself inject. Gemini CLI, however, reads files and supports MCP servers and stdin/stdout, so if a user bridges content from the list into prompts or MCP inputs, prompt injection becomes plausible. The pathway is not default between the pair, but Gemini’s permissive tool use raises the risk.
conditions: IF the operator copies content from awesome-nlp into Gemini CLI prompts or MCP-fed files
IF an MCP server returns attacker-controlled text that Gemini CLI treats as instructions
mitigations: Disable MCP servers for the session
Review copied text before pasting into Gemini CLI
Use a read-only workspace for any imported files
Add a prompt prefix that treats file contents as untrusted
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for external content

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-nlp touches no data classes and has no I/O, but Gemini CLI reads repo files and user-provided directories and can egress broadly to Google APIs and user-configured MCP servers. If sensitive files are placed in the shared workspace, Gemini can transmit them off-box. The pair does not prove leakage from A, but B’s default file-reading and egress make the workspace a realistic leak path.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the cwd or user-provided directories
IF Gemini CLI is allowed to call external APIs or MCP servers
mitigations: Keep sensitive files outside the Gemini workspace
Disable network egress for the session
Restrict MCP servers to trusted local endpoints
Use a throwaway clone with redacted inputs
requires-engineering: enforce per-directory data-loss controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-nlp has no write or execution capabilities, so it cannot contend for mutable state. Gemini CLI can write files, modify git state, execute shell, and spawn subprocesses, with shared state across instances via filesystem and git. If the pair is run in the same repo, Gemini can overwrite or race with other processes even though A itself is inert; uncertainty about orchestration means the safer medium rating is warranted.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI and another process share the same working tree
IF Gemini CLI is allowed to modify git state or write files in that tree
mitigations: Use separate working directories
Run Gemini CLI in a disposable clone
Avoid concurrent git operations
Lock the repo before edits
requires-engineering: add filesystem locking around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-nlp is a static resource, so it does not generate actions, but Gemini CLI can treat file contents and tool outputs as authoritative when composing code or shell actions. If content from the list is imported into Gemini’s context, Gemini may propagate errors or stale recommendations into downstream edits. The pair lacks direct evidence of automation, so this is not high, but the default trust-on-input pathway exists.
conditions: IF awesome-nlp content is used as source material for Gemini CLI outputs
IF Gemini CLI outputs are then copied into code, shell commands, or commits without verification
mitigations: Verify any derived facts before acting on them
Keep source lists separate from executable instructions
Require human review before commits
Use citations or links in generated outputs
requires-engineering: add output verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI or residency-sensitive data class is explicitly listed for awesome-nlp, so the main compliance issue is Gemini CLI’s handling of files, shell environment, and optional Google account login. If regulated data is placed in its workspace, broad egress and external API use can create retention or residency mismatches. The other agent is not a compliance source, so only Gemini is cited.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed in Gemini CLI’s workspace
IF the operator enables Google account login or external API access
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the workspace
Use a local-only account/session
Review retention settings before use
Disable external API calls
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
